84. **Mineral Blocks**: 4x `minecraft:copper_block`; 2x `minecraft:lapis_block`; 8x `minecraft:quartz_block` *(after: Building Tips, Nether Quartz)*
   > What: copper blocks weather from orange to green; lapis and quartz blocks are the classic blue and white trims.
   > Chemistry: copper turns green as it reacts with air, water and CO₂ into basic copper carbonate. Honeycomb wax stops it; an axe scrapes it back.
   > How: 9 copper ingots or 9 lapis per block; 4 Nether quartz per quartz block.
85. **Copper Craft**: 4x `minecraft:copper_grate`; 2x `minecraft:copper_bulb`; 4x `minecraft:chiseled_copper` *(after: Mineral Blocks)*
   > What: copper grates you can see through, copper bulbs that toggle with each redstone pulse, and chiseled copper.
   > Chemistry: in game a bulb dims as it weathers. Real patina (basic copper carbonate) is a far poorer conductor than the bright metal under it, which is why electrical contacts are kept clean.
   > How: cut copper blocks in a stonecutter; a bulb is copper blocks, a blaze rod and redstone (check JEI).
86. **Bars and Gates**: 16x `minecraft:iron_bars`; 2x `supplementaries:iron_gate` *(after: Mineral Blocks)*
   > What: iron bars make cages, windows and railings; Supplementaries iron gates open like fence gates.
   > Chemistry: iron rusts into hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·nH₂O; in game it never does, which is the only unrealistic thing about it.
   > How: six iron ingots make 16 bars (check JEI for the gate).
87. **Hulls and Supports**: 4x any of `or(item(createdeco:andesite_hull)item(createdeco:brass_hull)item(createdeco:copper_hull)item(createdeco:iron_hull)item(createdeco:zinc_hull)item(createdeco:industrial_iron_hull))`; 4x any of `or(item(createdeco:andesite_support)item(createdeco:brass_support)item(createdeco:copper_support)item(createdeco:iron_support)item(createdeco:zinc_support)item(createdeco:industrial_iron_support))` *(after: Mineral Blocks, Create Deco)*
   > What: hulls are riveted metal walls; supports are girders for roofs and catwalks.
   > How: any four hulls and four supports (check JEI).
   > Tip: copper hulls weather like copper blocks do. Wax them with honeycomb to keep the shine.
88. **Catwalks**: 8x any of `or(item(createdeco:andesite_catwalk)item(createdeco:brass_catwalk)item(createdeco:copper_catwalk)item(createdeco:iron_catwalk)item(createdeco:zinc_catwalk)item(createdeco:industrial_iron_catwalk))`; 4x any of `or(item(createdeco:andesite_catwalk_railing)item(createdeco:brass_catwalk_railing)item(createdeco:copper_catwalk_railing)item(createdeco:iron_catwalk_railing)item(createdeco:zinc_catwalk_railing)item(createdeco:industrial_iron_catwalk_railing))` *(after: Hulls and Supports)*
   > What: Create Deco catwalks and railings: see-through metal floors for walking over a factory.
   > How: any eight catwalks and four railings (check JEI).
   > Tip: catwalks over your pipes and belts keep everything reachable for repairs.
89. **Showing Off**: `minecraft:diamond_block` *(after: Mineral Blocks, Iron Tier)*
   > You remember a throne cut from a single gem. A block of diamond on the mantelpiece is a start.
   > What: a block of diamond, placed only to be looked at.
   > Chemistry: a block's worth of real diamond would be about 3.5 tonnes of pure carbon. Burn it and you'd get about 13 tonnes of CO₂.
90. **Laboratory Blocks**: 16x `laboratoryblocks:laboratory_block` *(after: Building Tips, Nether Quartz)*
   > You remember a laboratory of white stone and light. You can build it again.
   > What: Artemis' Laboratory Blocks adds clean lab walls, tiles, glass, screens, vents and fans.
   > Chemistry: the recipe uses Nether quartz, which is silicon dioxide (SiO₂), the same compound as sand and glass.
   > How: eight stone around one Nether quartz makes eight laboratory blocks (check JEI).
91. **Glowing Panels**: 8x `laboratoryblocks:glowstone_particles`; 8x `laboratoryblocks:glowing_laboratory_block` *(after: Laboratory Blocks)*
   > What: glowing laboratory blocks give off light, so a lab can be bright with no torches.
   > How: one glowstone dust makes eight glowstone particles; a particle plus a laboratory block makes a glowing block (check JEI).
   > Chemistry: real glow-in-the-dark materials store energy from light and release it slowly (phosphorescence).
92. **Lab Screens**: 4x any of `or(item(laboratoryblocks:clear_laboratory_screen)item(laboratoryblocks:text_laboratory_screen)item(laboratoryblocks:wave_laboratory_screen)item(laboratoryblocks:quantum_laboratory_screen)item(laboratoryblocks:glowing_clear_laboratory_screen)item(laboratoryblocks:glowing_text_laboratory_screen)item(laboratoryblocks:glowing_wave_laboratory_screen)item(laboratoryblocks:glowing_quantum_laboratory_screen))` *(after: Laboratory Blocks)*
   > What: decorative screens: clear, text, wave and quantum patterns, plain or glowing.
   > How: clear screens from laboratory blocks, laboratory glass and iron screws; add a dye for the patterns (check JEI).
   > Tip: put a wave screen beside your reactor and a ComputerCraft monitor next to it for real numbers.
93. **Fans and Vents**: `laboratoryblocks:laboratory_fan`; 2x `laboratoryblocks:laboratory_vent` *(after: Laboratory Blocks)*
   > What: animated lab fans and vents. The redstone-controlled fan only spins when powered.
   > Chemistry: real labs handle HCl, NH₃ and Cl₂ under a fume hood, which pulls vapours away from your face.
   > How: laboratory blocks with iron nuggets and iron screws (check JEI).
94. **Lab Doors and Glass**: 2x any of `or(item(laboratoryblocks:laboratory_door)item(laboratoryblocks:glass_laboratory_door)item(laboratoryblocks:mesh_laboratory_door))`; 8x `laboratoryblocks:laboratory_glass` *(after: Laboratory Blocks)*
   > What: lab doors (solid, glass or mesh) and laboratory glass for viewing windows.
   > How: doors from laboratory blocks; laboratory glass is eight glass around a laboratory block (check JEI).
   > Tip: a glass wall around your Alchemistry room lets visitors admire it without touching anything.
95. **Hazard Signs**: 3x any of `or(item(createdeco:decal_radioactive)item(createdeco:decal_fire_diamond)item(createdeco:decal_fire)item(createdeco:decal_warning)item(createdeco:decal_electrical)item(createdeco:decal_skull))` *(after: Laboratory Blocks, Create Deco)*
   > What: Create Deco decals: radiation, fire, electrical and warning signs to stick on walls and doors.
   > Chemistry: real labs label chemicals with hazard pictograms and the four-coloured fire diamond: blue for health, red for fire, yellow for reactivity, white for special hazards.
   > How: any three hazard decals (check JEI).
96. **A Proper Laboratory**: checkmark *(after: Glowing Panels, Lab Screens, Fans and Vents, Lab Doors and Glass)*
   > White walls, humming fans, glass and light. You remember this place. It was always where you were happiest.
   > What: a challenge: build a real laboratory around your chemistry machines with these blocks.
   > How: include glowing panels, screens, a fume fan and a glass wall. Click the checkmark when you're proud of it.

### Bounty Board

*Bounties on every monster. Each one is just chemistry with bad manners.*

1. **Zombie Hunter**: kill 25x `minecraft:zombie` *(after: Shield)*
   > You remember when the dead stayed down out of respect. Time to remind them.
   > What: the first bounty on the board. Each tier asks for more of the same mob and pays out a Hunter's Bounty.
   > How: zombies spawn in the dark and at night everywhere. A sword and shield are all you need.
   > Tip: zombies burn in daylight; fight at dawn and let the sun help.
2. **Zombie Slayer**: kill 100x `minecraft:zombie` *(after: Zombie Hunter)*
   > What: a hundred zombies. You'll get there just by playing at night.
   > Chemistry: rotten flesh really is rotten: bacteria break proteins into amines like putrescine and cadaverine, which is where the smell comes from.
   > Tip: a simple dark room over a spawner (YUNG's dungeons have plenty) speeds this up.
3. **Bane of the Dead**: kill 500x `minecraft:zombie` *(after: Zombie Slayer)*
   > What: five hundred. This one is for people who build mob farms.
   > How: a zombie spawner trap with a killing floor, or a Smite sword and a lot of nights.
   > Tip: Smite adds damage against all undead: zombies, skeletons, wither skeletons, phantoms and the Wither.
4. **Bone Collector**: kill 25x `minecraft:skeleton` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: skeletons drop bones and arrows, and sometimes their bow.
   > Chemistry: bone meal is crushed bone: calcium phosphate, a real phosphorus fertiliser for plants.
   > How: raise your shield when they draw, then close in between shots.
   > Tip: strafing sideways makes skeletons miss most of their arrows.
5. **Skeleton Slayer**: kill 100x `minecraft:skeleton` *(after: Bone Collector)*
   > What: a hundred skeletons, and a full stack of bones for bone meal.
   > How: keep killing them at night, or trap a skeleton spawner.
   > Tip: a skeleton spawner farm is also an arrow farm.
6. **Ossuary**: kill 500x `minecraft:skeleton` *(after: Skeleton Slayer)*
   > What: five hundred skeletons. Build a farm.
   > How: YUNG's skeleton dungeons have several spawners close together; trap them.
   > Tip: Looting raises bone and arrow drops.
7. **Undead of Every Climate**: kill 15x `minecraft:husk`; kill 15x `minecraft:stray`; kill 15x `minecraft:drowned` *(after: Zombie Hunter)*
   > What: the undead adapt to their biome: husks in deserts, strays in the snow, drowned in the water.
   > How: husks don't burn in daylight; strays shoot slowness arrows; drowned may carry tridents.
   > Tip: a drowned holding a trident can drop it. The trident is worth the hunt.
8. **Tide Breaker**: kill 100x `minecraft:drowned` *(after: Undead of Every Climate)*
   > What: a hundred drowned, for copper ingots, nautilus shells and the occasional trident.
   > Chemistry: fitting loot for the sea: copper resists seawater well, because it grows a protective skin of copper oxides and chlorides.
   > How: rivers and oceans at night. Channeling or Impaling help.
9. **Creeper Hunter**: kill 25x `minecraft:creeper` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: creepers drop gunpowder, the oldest chemical explosive.
   > Chemistry: gunpowder is potassium nitrate, charcoal and sulfur. The nitrate (KNO₃) supplies the oxygen: 2KNO₃ + S + 3C → K₂S + N₂ + 3CO₂.
   > How: hit and step back; a creeper resets its fuse when you leave its range.
   > Tip: a bow is the safest creeper tool there is.
10. **Demolition Expert**: kill 100x `minecraft:creeper` *(after: Creeper Hunter)*
   > What: a hundred creepers and a pile of gunpowder for TNT and rockets.
   > How: keep hunting at night; a Knockback sword keeps them away from you.
   > Tip: a creeper killed by a skeleton's arrow drops a music disc.
11. **Ssssilence**: kill 250x `minecraft:creeper` *(after: Demolition Expert)*
   > What: two hundred and fifty creepers. The world is quieter now.
   > How: a mob farm, or many careful nights.
   > Tip: cats scare creepers away from your base.
12. **Spider Hunter**: kill 25x `minecraft:spider` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: spiders drop string and spider eyes.
   > Chemistry: a fermented spider eye (eye + sugar + brown mushroom) turns potions into their opposites; real fermentation is microbes turning sugars into new compounds like ethanol and acids.
   > How: spiders climb walls; build with an overhang to keep them out.
   > Tip: spiders are neutral in daylight unless you hit them.
13. **Arachnophobe**: kill 100x `minecraft:spider` *(after: Spider Hunter)*
   > What: a hundred spiders, and enough string for every bow and wool block you need.
   > How: spiders spawn on the surface at night; Bane of Arthropods helps.
   > Tip: string from spiders makes wool: four string per block.
14. **Cave Spiders**: kill 25x `minecraft:cave_spider` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: small, poisonous spiders that only come from spawners in mineshafts and spider caves.
   > Chemistry: milk cures poison in Minecraft; in reality there's no general antidote, and venoms are treated with antivenom antibodies.
   > How: find a mineshaft or YUNG's spider cave and fight near the spawner. Carry milk.
   > Tip: torches on and around the spawner stop it.
15. **Pearl Diver**: kill 16x `minecraft:enderman` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: endermen drop ender pearls: teleportation, eyes of ender and many machines.
   > How: look at one to make it attack, then fight with your back to a 2-block-high gap; it can't follow under a low roof.
   > Tip: endermen hate water. A rain storm sends them teleporting away.
16. **Enderman Slayer**: kill 64x `minecraft:enderman` *(after: Pearl Diver)*
   > What: a stack of kills and, with luck, a stack of pearls.
   > How: warped forests in the Nether and the End are full of them.
   > Tip: a carved pumpkin on your head lets you look at endermen safely.
17. **Void Walker**: kill 256x `minecraft:enderman` *(after: Enderman Slayer)*
   > What: four stacks of endermen. You'll need an End farm or a lot of patience.
   > How: an enderman farm on the outer End islands is the classic way.
   > Tip: endermites make endermen aggressive; that's how most End farms lure them.
18. **Witch Hunt**: kill 10x `minecraft:witch` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: witches throw potions and drink their own to heal. They drop redstone, glowstone, sugar and bottles.
   > Chemistry: glowstone dust in-game is a brewing amplifier; real "glow" chemicals (like the zinc sulfide in glow paint) store light and release it slowly.
   > How: rush them; at range they out-potion you. Milk clears their effects.
   > Tip: swamp huts spawn witches over and over: a classic redstone farm.
19. **Coven Breaker**: kill 50x `minecraft:witch` *(after: Witch Hunt)*
   > What: fifty witches and a pile of redstone and glowstone.
   > How: a swamp hut farm, or raids (witches join them).
   > Tip: witches are immune to most potion damage; use a sword or bow.
20. **Slime Time**: kill 25x `minecraft:slime` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: slimes split when killed; the smallest drop slimeballs for sticky pistons and leads.
   > Chemistry: real slime is a polymer gel: long molecules cross-linked loosely enough to flow, like borax and PVA glue.
   > How: slimes spawn in swamps at night and in slime chunks underground.
   > Tip: every split counts as a kill. A big slime is many kills.
21. **Night Terrors**: kill 10x `minecraft:phantom` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: phantoms dive at players who haven't slept for three nights. Their membranes repair elytra.
   > How: stay up three nights, then fight with a bow on open ground at night.
   > Tip: once you're done, sleep: it resets the timer and phantoms stop coming.
22. **Skyclearer**: kill 50x `minecraft:phantom` *(after: Night Terrors)*
   > What: fifty phantoms, and enough membranes to keep an elytra flying for a long time.
   > How: a bow with Power, or a trident with Loyalty, and a sleepless week.
   > Tip: phantoms are undead; Smite works on them.
23. **Pest Control**: kill 50x `minecraft:silverfish` *(after: Cave Spiders)*
   > What: silverfish hide in infested stone in strongholds and mountains, and call their friends when hurt.
   > How: YUNG's strongholds are full of infested blocks; a single blow kills each one.
   > Tip: don't break blocks near a silverfish fight; you'll wake more.
24. **The Trials**: kill 10x `minecraft:breeze`; kill 10x `minecraft:bogged` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: two mobs from 1.21: breezes (wind spirits) and bogged (mossy skeletons with poison arrows), both from trial chambers.
   > How: find a trial chamber (see the Exploration page) and fight the trial spawners.
   > Tip: breeze rods make wind charges and the mace.
25. **Pillager Hunter**: kill 25x `minecraft:pillager` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: crossbow-armed illagers from outposts and patrols.
   > How: a shield blocks their bolts. Outposts respawn pillagers around the tower.
   > Tip: a captain (banner on its head) gives Bad Omen when killed: drink the ominous bottle to start a raid.
26. **Outpost Breaker**: kill 100x `minecraft:pillager` *(after: Pillager Hunter)*
   > What: a hundred pillagers.
   > How: camp an outpost or run raids. Raids bring them in waves.
   > Tip: a raid farm is the best emerald source in the game.
27. **Axes of Malice**: kill 10x `minecraft:vindicator` *(after: Pillager Hunter)*
   > What: axe-wielding illagers from raids and woodland mansions. They hit very hard.
   > How: keep your shield up; their axes can disable it, so back off after a block.
   > Tip: a vindicator named "Johnny" attacks every mob in sight.
28. **Evoker Bane**: kill 3x `minecraft:evoker` *(after: Axes of Malice)*
   > What: evokers summon fangs and vexes. Each one drops a Totem of Undying.
   > How: they come in later raid waves and live in woodland mansions. Kill the evoker first; its vexes die with it.
   > Tip: keep a totem in your off-hand when fighting raids.
29. **Beast of the Raid**: kill 3x `minecraft:ravager` *(after: Axes of Malice)*
   > What: ravagers are huge raid beasts that trample crops and charge.
   > How: they appear in raids from wave 3 on. Block the charge with a shield, then counterattack while it's stunned.
   > Tip: ravagers drop saddles.
30. **Guardian Hunter**: kill 25x `minecraft:guardian` *(after: Shield)*
   > What: the spiky fish of ocean monuments. They drop prismarine shards and crystals.
   > Chemistry: prismarine is in-game sea crystal; real sea creatures build shells and spines from calcium carbonate and silica pulled out of seawater.
   > How: find a monument (see the Exploration page). Break line of sight when their laser charges.
   > Tip: water breathing and Depth Strider make monuments much easier.
31. **Gold in the Rot**: kill 50x `minecraft:zombified_piglin` *(after: Into the Fire)*
   > What: zombified piglins drop gold nuggets and rotten flesh.
   > How: they're neutral until you hit one, then the whole crowd comes. Fight in a corridor.
   > Tip: gold farms over Nether-roof portals are a classic build.
32. **Blaze Hunter**: kill 25x `minecraft:blaze` *(after: Into the Fire)*
   > What: blazes drop blaze rods: brewing stands, blaze powder and eyes of ender.
   > Chemistry: blazes throw fireballs; real fireballs need fuel plus oxygen, which is why a fire triangle (heat, fuel, O₂) puts them out when you remove any side.
   > How: blaze spawners sit in Nether fortresses. Snowballs hurt them.
   > Tip: fire resistance makes you immune to their fireballs.
33. **Blaze Slayer**: kill 100x `minecraft:blaze` *(after: Blaze Hunter)*
   > What: a hundred blazes and a good supply of rods.
   > How: build a blaze farm around a fortress spawner.
   > Tip: blaze rods are a good furnace fuel: 12 items each.
34. **Ghastbuster**: kill 10x `minecraft:ghast` *(after: Into the Fire)*
   > What: ghasts drop ghast tears (regeneration potions, end crystals) and gunpowder.
   > How: hit their fireballs back at them with a sword or an arrow.
   > Tip: kill them over solid ground, not lava, or the tear is lost.
35. **Hot Jelly**: kill 50x `minecraft:magma_cube` *(after: Into the Fire)*
   > What: magma cubes split like slimes and drop magma cream for fire resistance.
   > How: basalt deltas are full of them.
   > Tip: every split counts as a kill.
36. **Skull Hunter**: kill 25x `minecraft:wither_skeleton` *(after: Into the Fire)*
   > What: tall black skeletons in Nether fortresses. They sometimes drop their skull; three summon the Wither.
   > How: fight in a 2-block-high tunnel; they're three blocks tall and can't follow.
   > Tip: Looting raises the skull drop chance.
37. **Bonebreaker**: kill 100x `minecraft:wither_skeleton` *(after: Skull Hunter)*
   > What: a hundred wither skeletons, and enough skulls for several Withers.
   > How: a wither skeleton farm on a fortress platform.
   > Tip: a Smite sword kills them quickly.
38. **Bastion Brawl**: kill 5x `minecraft:piglin_brute`; kill 10x `minecraft:hoglin` *(after: Into the Fire)*
   > What: the toughest regular Nether fighters: axe-armed piglin brutes in bastions and charging hoglins in crimson forests.
   > Chemistry: hoglins fear warped fungus; real animals avoid many plant compounds, which evolved as chemical defences.
   > How: brutes ignore gold armour; fight them in doorways. Hoglins drop pork and leather.
   > Tip: hoglins turn into zoglins in the Overworld, so don't bring one home.
39. **Shell Game**: kill 20x `minecraft:shulker` *(after: The End)*
   > What: shulkers hide in End Cities and drop shells for shulker boxes.
   > How: hit them when their shell opens. Their bullets make you levitate.
   > Tip: carry milk or slow falling against levitation.
40. **The Rotspawn**: kill 20x `undergarden:rotling`; kill 10x `undergarden:rotwalker`; kill 3x `undergarden:rotbeast` *(after: The Undergarden)*
   > What: the Undergarden's undead-like rotspawn: small rotlings, tall rotwalkers and the huge rotbeast.
   > How: utherium weapons deal extra damage to rotspawn.
   > Tip: rotbeasts hit hard and have a lot of health; fight them in the open.
41. **Things in the Dark**: kill 5x `undergarden:nargoyle`; kill 10x `undergarden:muncher` *(after: The Undergarden)*
   > What: more Undergarden predators: nargoyles and the hungry munchers.
   > How: explore the Undergarden at length; both turn up in its caverns.
   > Tip: cloggrum armour is the Undergarden's best early protection.
42. **Sculk Fauna**: kill 10x `deeperdarker:sculk_snapper`; kill 10x `deeperdarker:sculk_centipede` *(after: The Otherside)*
   > What: creatures of the Otherside, grown from sculk.
   > How: roam the Otherside's biomes. Sneak to approach without alerting the sculk.
   > Tip: carry food and a way home; the Otherside is a long way from your base.
43. **Shattered and Stalkers**: kill 10x `deeperdarker:shattered`; kill 3x `deeperdarker:stalker` *(after: Sculk Fauna)*
   > What: shattered drop sculk bones; stalkers drop soul crystals. Both go into the soul elytra.
   > How: both hunt by sound like the Warden. Fight at range.
   > Tip: sneak to keep your footsteps quiet.
44. **Martian Raptors**: kill 10x `ad_astra:martian_raptor` *(after: Mars)*
   > What: fast predators of the Martian surface.
   > Chemistry: anything living on Mars would need to cope with perchlorates (ClO₄⁻), reactive salts found in real Martian soil.
   > How: land on Mars and hunt in the wastelands. Keep your suit topped up.
45. **Twilight Pests**: kill 20x `twilightforest:redcap`; kill 20x `twilightforest:kobold`; kill 20x `twilightforest:swarm_spider` *(after: The Twilight Forest)*
   > What: the common hostile mobs of the Twilight Forest.
   > How: redcaps and kobolds roam the forest; swarm spiders spawn around hollow hills and spider-infested spots.
   > Tip: redcap sappers carry TNT; kill them before they light it.
46. **Maze and Swamp**: kill 10x `twilightforest:minotaur`; kill 10x `twilightforest:maze_slime`; kill 10x `twilightforest:skeleton_druid` *(after: The Lich)*
   > What: guardians of the labyrinth and the swamp beyond the Lich.
   > How: minotaurs and maze slimes fill the labyrinth; skeleton druids lurk in the forest at night.
   > Tip: maze slimes split like regular slimes.
47. **Goblins and Ghastguards**: kill 10x `twilightforest:lower_goblin_knight`; kill 5x `twilightforest:blockchain_goblin`; kill 10x `twilightforest:carminite_ghastguard` *(after: The Hydra)*
   > What: goblin knights and block-and-chain goblins hold the Goblin Stronghold; carminite ghastguards haunt the Dark Tower.
   > How: goblin knights ride in pairs; knock off the upper one, then finish the lower.
   > Tip: ghastguards' fireballs can be hit back like a ghast's.
48. **Snow Beasts**: kill 10x `twilightforest:yeti`; kill 10x `twilightforest:winter_wolf` *(after: The Lich)*
   > What: the snowy forest's hunters. Yetis drop arctic fur for warm armour.
   > How: yetis guard the Alpha Yeti's cave; winter wolves roam the snowy forest and breathe frost.
   > Tip: winter wolves come in packs; back against a tree.
49. **Trolls and Giants**: kill 5x `twilightforest:troll`; kill 3x `twilightforest:giant_miner` *(after: The Highlands)*
   > What: trolls in the troll caves and giant miners on the highlands.
   > How: trolls throw rocks; giants swing slowly but hard. Fight both from range.
   > Tip: giant miners drop giant pickaxes.
50. **Elder Guardians**: kill 3x `minecraft:elder_guardian` *(after: Guardian Hunter)*
   > What: each ocean monument holds three elder guardians. They cast Mining Fatigue until all three are dead.
   > How: the elders sit in the top room and two wing rooms. Water breathing, a good sword and patience.
   > Tip: elders drop wet sponges and, sometimes, a tide armour trim.
51. **The Wither**: kill 1x `minecraft:wither`; `minecraft:nether_star` *(after: Skull Hunter)*
   > You remember making stars. This one you'll have to take.
   > What: the Wither is the Nether's boss, summoned by the player. It drops a Nether Star for beacons and many late recipes.
   > How: four soul sand in a T with three wither skeleton skulls on top. Summon it deep underground or far from base: it destroys blocks.
   > Tip: below half health it gains armour that stops arrows; switch to a Smite sword.
52. **Web Breaker**: kill 250x `minecraft:spider` *(after: Arachnophobe)*
   > What: two hundred and fifty spiders. Every web in the world is a little emptier.
   > Chemistry: spider silk is a protein whose chains line up into tiny crystals; weight for weight it is tougher than steel.
   > How: a spider spawner farm, or long nights on the surface with Bane of Arthropods.
53. **Hexbreaker**: kill 100x `minecraft:witch` *(after: Coven Breaker)*
   > What: a hundred witches, and enough redstone and glowstone to light a city.
   > How: a swamp hut farm is the only sane way; raids help too.
   > Tip: witches drink fire resistance when burning, so lava traps work poorly on them.
54. **Flame Tamer**: kill 250x `minecraft:blaze` *(after: Blaze Slayer)*
   > What: two hundred and fifty blazes: a lifetime supply of rods for brewing and fuel.
   > Chemistry: a blaze is fire you can kill. Real fire is just a fast oxidation reaction feeding on its own heat.
   > How: a blaze spawner farm in a fortress, with a killing floor and a collector.
55. **Skullcrusher**: kill 250x `minecraft:wither_skeleton` *(after: Bonebreaker)*
   > What: two hundred and fifty wither skeletons, and a crate of skulls.
   > How: a wither skeleton farm on a cleared fortress platform; the skeletons spawn on nether bricks.
   > Tip: coal and stone swords from them are worth smelting or dissolving, not keeping.
56. **Moon Raiders**: kill 10x `ad_astra:corrupted_lunarian`; kill 10x `ad_astra:star_crawler` *(after: Desh on the Moon)*
   > What: the Moon's wastelands are home to corrupted lunarians and star crawlers. Both attack on sight.
   > Chemistry: the Moon has no air to carry sound or heat, so a fight there is silent and the sun side of a rock is scorching.
   > How: land on the Moon and roam the lunar wastelands. Keep your suit's oxygen topped up.
57. **Venusian Hunt**: kill 10x `ad_astra:sulfur_creeper`; kill 5x `ad_astra:mogler`; kill 10x `ad_astra:zombified_pygro` *(after: Venus)*
   > What: Venus's barrens crawl with sulfur creepers, charging moglers and zombified pygros.
   > Chemistry: real Venus has clouds of sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) over a 460 °C surface, which is why its creepers come in sulfur.
   > How: land on Venus in a heat-shielded suit and hunt the wastelands. Fight on solid ground away from the lava.
58. **Spoils: Rotten Flesh**: 32x `minecraft:rotten_flesh` *(after: Zombie Hunter)*
   > What: a stack of rotten flesh. Nobody wants to eat it, but your Dissolver does.
   > Chemistry: the Dissolver breaks one rotten flesh into 3 protein. Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds (–CO–NH–); rotting is bacteria cutting those chains.
   > How: keep the flesh from your zombie hunts instead of throwing it away.
   > Tip: dissolve the protein again and it gives ammonia, CO₂, ethylene and sulfur; the sulfur comes from the amino acids cysteine and methionine.
59. **Spoils: Bones**: 32x `minecraft:bone` *(after: Bone Collector)*
   > What: a stack of bones: bone meal, bone blocks and a mineral the Dissolver can use.
   > Chemistry: bone is mostly hydroxyapatite, Ca₅(PO₄)₃OH. Half the time the Dissolver gives 3 of it per bone: calcium and phosphorus in one crystal.
   > How: keep the bones from skeletons.
   > Tip: hydroxyapatite is also what tooth enamel is made of; fluoride toothpaste swaps OH⁻ for F⁻ to make it harder.
60. **Spoils: Silk and Eyes**: 32x `minecraft:string`; 8x `minecraft:spider_eye` *(after: Spider Hunter)*
   > What: string for bows, wool and machines, and spider eyes for brewing.
   > Chemistry: in the Dissolver, string gives keratin and a spider eye gives beta-carotene and chitin. Real spider silk is a different protein, spidroin, and is tougher than steel for its weight.
   > How: keep the drops from your spider hunts. Witches drop spider eyes too.
   > Tip: beta-carotene is the orange pigment in carrots; your body splits it into vitamin A.
61. **Spoils: The Witch's Pantry**: 8x `minecraft:glowstone_dust`; 8x `minecraft:sugar`; 4x `minecraft:glass_bottle` *(after: Witch Hunt)*
   > What: the ingredients witches carry: glowstone dust, sugar and empty bottles.
   > Chemistry: the Dissolver breaks glowstone dust into 4 phosphorus and sugar into sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Glass itself is mostly SiO₂, melted with soda (Na₂CO₃) and lime so it softens at a workable heat.
   > How: keep the drops from witches; swamp huts respawn them.
   > Tip: sucrose in the Dissolver is one of the easiest early sources of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
62. **The Trident**: `minecraft:trident` *(after: Undead of Every Climate)*
   > What: the only trident in the game is the one a drowned carries. It can't be crafted.
   > How: fight drowned in rivers and oceans; only those holding a trident can drop one, and it's rare. Looting helps.
   > Tip: enchant it with Loyalty to have it fly back, Riptide to launch yourself in rain, or Channeling to call lightning.

### Lab Notebook

*Why it works: the real chemistry behind every machine in the pack.*

1. **Note: Why Alloys Are Harder**: checkmark *(after: The First Alloy)*
   > You open a notebook in your own handwriting. The first page is about bronze.
   > What: a pure metal is soft because its atoms sit in neat layers that slide past each other.
   > Chemistry: add a few bigger or smaller atoms (tin in copper) and the layers jam. Bronze is about 88% Cu, 12% Sn.
   > Tip: tick this when you've read both pages. Lab notes never block the main path.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Deep dive: metals are a lattice of positive ions in a 'sea' of shared electrons (metallic bonding). The electrons hold the ions together but let whole planes of atoms shift: that's why metals bend instead of shattering.
   > Solid solutions: in bronze, tin atoms replace some copper atoms in the lattice. Tin atoms are larger, so they distort the planes around them and pin them in place. Harder, stronger, still workable.
   > In the pack: 3 copper dust + 1 tin dust → 3 bronze dust (a 3:1 ratio by count, close to the historical recipe). Every later alloy follows the same idea with different partners.
2. **Note: Steel and Carbon**: checkmark *(after: Steel)*
   > What: steel is iron with up to about 2% carbon. Most structural steel has well under 1%.
   > Chemistry: tiny carbon atoms fit into the gaps between iron atoms (an interstitial alloy) and lock the layers.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > From ore to iron: a real blast furnace burns coke to carbon monoxide, which strips oxygen from iron ore: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.
   > Too much carbon: furnace iron ('pig iron') has about 4% carbon and is brittle. Steelmaking blows oxygen through it to burn the excess off as CO and CO₂ (the basic oxygen process).
   > In the pack: MI skips the ore step: iron dust + coke dust → uncooked steel, baked in the Steam Blast Furnace. The coke you made is the carbon source.
3. **Note: Invar, the Metal That Won't Grow**: checkmark *(after: Electric Mixer)*
   > What: invar is about 64% iron and 36% nickel. MI uses it for rotary blades and gears.
   > Chemistry: most metals expand when heated. Invar barely does, which keeps precision parts precise.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Why: in this exact mix, a magnetic effect inside the crystal shrinks the lattice as it warms, cancelling the normal expansion (the 'Invar effect').
   > History: Charles-Édouard Guillaume found it in 1896 and won the 1920 Nobel Prize in Physics. It went into clocks, measuring tapes and later the shadow masks of colour TVs.
   > In the pack: mix iron and nickel dust in the Mixer (check JEI for the ratio). Cupronickel (copper + nickel) is its cousin, used for heating coils because it resists current steadily.
4. **Note: Electrum, a Natural Alloy**: checkmark *(after: Electrum)*
   > What: electrum is gold alloyed with silver. It's found that way in rivers, already mixed.
   > Chemistry: gold and silver atoms are almost the same size and both form the same crystal, so they mix in any proportion.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Complete solubility: when two metals have similar atomic radius, the same crystal structure and similar electronegativity, they can blend smoothly from 0% to 100% (the Hume-Rothery rules). Gold-silver and copper-nickel are classic examples.
   > Why MI wants it: both metals conduct electricity superbly and resist corrosion, ideal for circuit boards.
   > In the pack: gold ore often gives silver as a byproduct in the Centrifuge for exactly this reason: native gold is usually electrum.
5. **Note: Stainless Steel**: checkmark *(after: Stainless Steel)*
   > What: steel with at least 10.5% chromium (plus nickel and manganese) that doesn't rust.
   > Chemistry: chromium reacts with air to form a thin Cr₂O₃ film only a few atoms thick. It seals the surface.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Passivation: ordinary rust (hydrated iron oxide) is flaky, so it falls off and exposes fresh iron: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2xH₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Chromium oxide is dense and sticks, so oxygen can't get through.
   > Self-repair: scratch the surface and the exposed chromium reacts with oxygen again within moments, rebuilding the film.
   > In the pack: 6 iron + 1 chromium + 1 nickel + 1 manganese dust → 9 stainless dust. It melts so hot that it leaves the EBF as a hot ingot and must be cooled in the Vacuum Freezer.
6. **Note: Coking Coal**: checkmark *(after: Coke)*
   > What: coke is coal heated in an oven with no air, leaving almost pure carbon.
   > Chemistry: without oxygen the coal can't burn. Instead its volatile parts (tars, gases, water) boil away. This is pyrolysis.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > What leaves: coal tar and creosote (heavy aromatic oils), coal gas (mostly H₂ and CH₄), ammonia and sulfur compounds. Old gasworks sold all of them.
   > What stays: a hard, porous carbon skeleton. It's strong enough to carry the weight of ore in a blast furnace and burns hotter than coal.
   > In the pack: the Coke Oven turns coal into coke and sometimes creosote. Charcoal from wood is the same idea on a smaller scale.
7. **Note: Taking Things Apart**: checkmark *(after: The Dissolver)*
   > What: the Dissolver turns any block into the elements and compounds it's made of.
   > Chemistry: every substance is built from about 90 natural elements. Analysing what's inside is called elemental analysis.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > The real thing: chemists can't dissolve a block of wood into a pile of carbon, but they can measure it. Burn a sample in oxygen and weigh the CO₂ and H₂O formed: that gives the carbon and hydrogen content (combustion analysis). A mass spectrometer reads atoms by their mass.
   > Conservation of mass: atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical change, only rearranged (Lavoisier, 1789). The Dissolver is a game version of that law: everything you put in comes out as atoms.
   > In the pack: many outputs are chance-based (JEI shows the odds). Some items give compounds first; dissolve those again for pure elements.
8. **Note: Fixed Recipes**: checkmark *(after: The Combiner)*
   > What: the Combiner always needs the same numbers of each element for a compound.
   > Chemistry: that's the law of definite proportions: a pure compound always has the same elements in the same ratio.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Proust's law (1794): water from a river, a glacier or a test tube is always 2 H for every 1 O, which is 11.2% hydrogen by mass. Compounds aren't mixtures; they have a formula.
   > Balanced equations: because atoms are conserved, both sides of a reaction must hold the same atoms: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 4 H and 2 O on each side. The Combiner's recipes are balanced equations made of items.
   > In the pack: compare a Combiner recipe in JEI with the formula on the compound's tooltip; the counts match.
9. **Note: Isotopes**: checkmark *(after: Isotope Separation)*
   > What: isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
   > Chemistry: chemistry is decided by electrons, and isotopes have the same electrons, so they react identically. Only their mass differs.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Hydrogen's three: ¹H (no neutron), deuterium ²H (one) and tritium ³H (two). Deuterium is stable and found in heavy water, D₂O; tritium is radioactive and is bred from lithium. Both feed the fusion reactor.
   > Uranium's two: natural uranium is 99.3% U-238 and only 0.72% U-235, the isotope that splits easily. Reactors need it enriched to roughly 3 to 5%.
   > How enrichment works: turn uranium into UF₆, a gas, then spin it. Molecules with U-238 are about 1% heavier and drift outward. Thousands of centrifuges in a row (a cascade) multiply that tiny difference. The Isotopic Centrifuge is one stage of that.
10. **Note: Making Elements**: checkmark *(after: Element Transmutation)*
   > What: Alchemistry's fission and fusion chambers split or join nuclei to change one element into another.
   > Chemistry: an element is defined by its proton count (atomic number). Change the nucleus and you change the element. That's nuclear physics, not chemistry.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > In stars: stars fuse hydrogen into helium, then helium into carbon and oxygen, and so on up to iron. Fusing past iron costs energy instead of releasing it.
   > Heavier than iron: most heavy elements form when nuclei capture neutrons, slowly in old giant stars (the s-process) or in a flash during neutron-star mergers and supernovae (the r-process). Your gold was forged in a cosmic collision.
   > Oganesson (118): made in 2002 by firing calcium-48 (Z = 20) at californium-249 (Z = 98): 20 + 98 = 118. Only a handful of atoms have ever existed, each lasting under a millisecond. The chambers add atomic numbers the same way.
11. **Fool's Gold**: `chemlib:iron_disulfide` *(after: The Combiner)*
   > You remember laughing at prospectors. Then you remember being one.
   > What: you synthesised iron disulfide, FeS₂: pyrite, better known as fool's gold.
   > Chemistry: brassy and cubic, it fooled miners for centuries. Strike it on steel and it sparks; the name comes from the Greek for fire.
   > Tip: roasting pyrite was once a major source of SO₂ for sulfuric acid: 4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂.
12. **Note: Why Crushing Doubles Ore**: checkmark *(after: Steam Macerator)*
   > What: in this pack, every route caps at 2x per ore block (1.5x per raw ore) until you have acids.
   > Chemistry: real ore is a little metal mineral locked in a lot of worthless rock (gangue). Grinding frees the mineral so it can be separated.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Beneficiation: mines crush ore to powder, then concentrate it. Dense minerals sink in water (gravity separation), magnetic ones stick to magnets, and sulfide minerals cling to air bubbles in froth flotation while the rock sinks.
   > Smelting the concentrate: only then is the metal freed by heat and chemistry, for example 2PbS + 3O₂ → 2PbO + 2SO₂, then PbO + C → Pb + CO.
   > The game rule: crushing recovers more of the metal than tossing raw chunks in a furnace, so dust gives more ingots. The 2x cap is a balance choice; the next notes explain how acids push past it.
13. **Note: 3x, 4x, 5x**: checkmark *(after: 5x Ore: Dissolution)*
   > What: Mekanism's ore chain adds a chemical step per tier: O₂ (3x), HCl (4x), H₂SO₄ (5x).
   > Chemistry: each step mirrors a real way of pulling metal out of rock: roasting, chlorination and leaching.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > 3x, oxygen: roasting sulfide ore in air turns it into an oxide that is easier to reduce: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂.
   > 4x, chloride: metal chlorides are often volatile or soluble, so chlorination separates metals cleanly. Titanium is refined this way (the Kroll process goes through TiCl₄).
   > 5x, leaching: sulfuric acid dissolves the metal out as a sulfate slurry, e.g. CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. Wash it, crystallise it, and almost nothing is left behind. This hydrometallurgy is how much of the world's copper is made today.
14. **Note: Ores Come in Families**: checkmark *(after: Ore Byproducts)*
   > What: centrifuging Mekanism dirty dust gives the main metal plus a chance at a second one.
   > Chemistry: metals with similar chemistry crystallise together in the same rocks, so real refineries recover them as byproducts.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > The pairs in this pack: iron → nickel (iron-nickel ores), copper → gold (recovered when copper is refined), gold → silver (native gold is electrum), lead → silver (galena, PbS, is the main silver source), tin → tungsten (cassiterite sits with wolframite), osmium → iridium (osmiridium), uranium → lead (uranium decays into lead over billions of years).
   > Why it matters: many rare metals have no mines of their own. Most of the world's indium, gallium and germanium comes out of zinc and aluminum refining.
15. **Note: Refining Platinum**: checkmark *(after: The Platinum Line)*
   > What: the platinum line turns anode sludge into pure platinum and four rarer metals.
   > Chemistry: platinum resists almost every acid, but aqua regia (3 HCl : 1 HNO₃) dissolves it. Then a salt pulls it back out alone.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Step 1, dissolve: nitric acid oxidises the metal and chloride holds it in solution: Pt + 4HNO₃ + 6HCl → H₂PtCl₆ + 4NO₂ + 4H₂O.
   > Step 2, precipitate: ammonium chloride forms a yellow salt that barely dissolves: H₂PtCl₆ + 2NH₄Cl → (NH₄)₂PtCl₆ + 2HCl.
   > Step 3, calcine: heat drives everything else off as gas: 3(NH₄)₂PtCl₆ → 3Pt + 2NH₄Cl + 16HCl + 2N₂.
   > The residue: iridium, osmium, rhodium and ruthenium don't dissolve in aqua regia, so they stay behind and are separated later (the Centrifuge in this pack).
16. **Coffee Break**: checkmark *(after: The Combiner)*
   > Moved: this step is now "Morning Coffee" on the The Periodic Table page. Click to dismiss.
17. **Note: Splitting Water**: checkmark *(after: Mekanism Gases)*
   > What: the Electrolytic Separator (and MI's Electrolyzer) split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
   > Chemistry: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Burning hydrogen releases energy; electrolysis pays that energy back to undo it.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > At the electrodes: the negative electrode (cathode) gives electrons to water: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻. The positive electrode (anode) takes them: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
   > Two to one: twice as much hydrogen gas as oxygen comes off, by volume, exactly as the formula says. MI matches it: 3000 mB water → 2000 mB H₂ + 1000 mB O₂.
   > Real detail: pure water barely conducts, so real cells add a dissolved salt or alkali (an electrolyte) to carry the current. Only the water is used up.
18. **Note: The Chlor-Alkali Process**: checkmark *(after: Chlorine)*
   > What: electrolysing salt gives chlorine, one of the most-used industrial chemicals (PVC, bleach, HCl).
   > Chemistry: in water: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → Cl₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH. Molten salt with no water gives metal: 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Two routes: brine cells (the chlor-alkali process) make chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide (lye) together. Molten-salt cells (the Downs cell) make sodium metal and chlorine. Mekanism's separator gives sodium + chlorine, like the Downs cell.
   > Why chlorine goes to the anode: chloride ions (Cl⁻) carry the negative charge, so they're drawn to the positive electrode and give up their electrons: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
   > Next step: hydrogen and chlorine combine into hydrogen chloride, H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, which you need for 4x ore and for PVC.
19. **Note: Catalysts**: checkmark *(after: Contact Process 2: SO₃)*
   > What: a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being consumed. Industry runs on them.
   > Chemistry: it offers an easier pathway with a lower energy barrier (activation energy). It doesn't change where the equilibrium ends up.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Classic catalysts: vanadium(V) oxide for SO₂ → SO₃ (contact process), iron for ammonia (Haber-Bosch), platinum-rhodium gauze for burning ammonia (Ostwald), chromium or titanium compounds for polyethylene, and zeolites in refinery cat-crackers.
   > Surface catalysts: gases stick to the metal surface, their bonds weaken, they react, and the product lets go, freeing the site for the next molecule.
   > In the pack: machines don't model catalysts, and MI's polymer recipes consume a few tiny metal dusts. In real plants the catalyst is replaced only when it slowly wears out or gets poisoned.
20. **Note: The Contact Process**: checkmark *(after: Contact Process 3: H₂SO₄)*
   > What: sulfuric acid is made in larger amounts than any other chemical: about 250 million tonnes a year.
   > Chemistry: S + O₂ → SO₂, then 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅, then SO₃ is turned into H₂SO₄.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > The balancing act: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ releases heat, so lower temperatures give more SO₃ but react slowly. About 450 °C with a catalyst is the compromise. This is Le Chatelier's principle in action.
   > The odd last step: SO₃ isn't bubbled straight into water; that makes a fine acid mist. It's absorbed into existing concentrated acid to form oleum (H₂S₂O₇), which is then diluted: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.
   > In the pack: Mekanism splits the steps across three machines; MI's Chemical Reactor does it all at once from sulfur, oxygen and water. Its uses: 5x ore, fertilisers, batteries and the Seed of a New World.
21. **Note: Haber-Bosch**: checkmark *(after: Haber-Bosch)*
   > What: ammonia, NH₃, made from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen. Fertiliser made from it feeds billions.
   > Chemistry: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. The N≡N triple bond is one of the strongest bonds there is, so it needs pressure, heat and an iron catalyst.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Conditions: about 200 atmospheres and 400 to 450 °C over iron. The reaction releases heat, so cooler gives more ammonia but far too slowly; high pressure helps because 4 gas molecules become 2.
   > Recycling: only about 15% converts per pass, so the ammonia is condensed out and the unreacted gas goes round again.
   > Real hydrogen: most comes from natural gas (steam reforming, CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂). In the pack you get it from electrolysis instead, the 'green ammonia' route.
22. **Note: The Ostwald Process**: checkmark *(after: Ostwald Process)*
   > What: nitric acid, HNO₃, for fertiliser, explosives in mining, and in this pack, aqua regia.
   > Chemistry: overall NH₃ + 2O₂ → HNO₃ + H₂O, which happens in three real steps.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Step 1: ammonia burns over a red-hot platinum-rhodium gauze (about 900 °C): 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O. The contact lasts only milliseconds.
   > Step 2: the gas cools and nitric oxide picks up more oxygen: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (brown).
   > Step 3: NO₂ is absorbed in water: 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO. The leftover NO goes back to step 2.
   > In the pack: the Chemical Reactor does all three at once: 1 B ammonia + 2 B oxygen → 1 B nitric acid + 1 B water.
23. **Note: Fractional Distillation**: checkmark *(after: Fractional Distillation)*
   > What: crude oil is a mix of thousands of hydrocarbons. A distillation tower sorts them into fractions.
   > Chemistry: bigger molecules have stronger attractions between them, so they boil at higher temperatures.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > The tower: crude is heated to about 400 °C and fed in near the bottom. Vapour rises through trays, cooling as it goes; each fraction condenses at the height where the tower matches its boiling point.
   > Top to bottom: refinery gas (C₁ to C₄), naphtha (about C₅ to C₁₀), kerosene, diesel (light fuel), fuel oil (heavy fuel), and a tarry residue at the base.
   > Sour crude: crude contains sulfur compounds, which is why MI's first fractions are 'sulfuric'. Hydrotreating with hydrogen strips the sulfur out as H₂S, and in MI that comes back to you as sulfuric acid.
24. **Note: Steam Cracking**: checkmark *(after: Steam Cracking)*
   > What: cracking breaks big, less useful molecules into small, valuable ones, especially ethylene.
   > Chemistry: e.g. C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. One product must have a C=C double bond, because there isn't enough hydrogen to go round.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Steam cracking: naphtha mixed with steam is heated to about 850 °C for a fraction of a second, then quenched. The steam dilutes the hydrocarbon so it doesn't coke up the pipes. No catalyst: heat alone snaps the C-C bonds.
   > Catalytic cracking: refineries also crack heavy oil over zeolite catalysts at lower temperatures to make petrol. That's a different process with a different goal.
   > In the pack: naphtha + steam → steam-cracked naphtha in the Chemical Reactor, then the Distillation Tower separates ethylene, propene, benzene and more.
25. **Note: Polymers**: checkmark *(after: Polymerisation)*
   > What: a polymer is a giant molecule made of repeating small units (monomers). Polyethylene is the world's most common plastic.
   > Chemistry: n C₂H₄ → (-CH₂-CH₂-)ₙ. Each double bond opens and links to the next molecule: addition polymerisation.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Chain length: a typical polyethylene chain has tens of thousands of carbon atoms. Long chains tangle like spaghetti, which is why plastic is tough instead of waxy.
   > LDPE vs HDPE: high-pressure, radical polymerisation gives branched chains that pack loosely (soft LDPE film). Metal catalysts (Ziegler-Natta, Phillips) give straight chains that pack tightly (stiff HDPE, Mekanism's HDPE pellets).
   > In the pack: polyethylene unlocks HV digital circuits, and 16 buckets go into the Seed of a New World.
26. **Note: PVC**: checkmark *(after: PVC)*
   > What: polyvinyl chloride, the plastic of pipes, cable insulation and window frames. MI needs it for EV processing units.
   > Chemistry: n C₂H₃Cl → (-CH₂-CHCl-)ₙ. The same addition polymerisation as polyethylene, with one H swapped for Cl.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Why chlorine matters: the C-Cl bonds make PVC rigid, oil-resistant and slow to burn (it releases HCl, which smothers flames). That's why it's trusted around electrical wiring.
   > Making the monomer: the old route, used in MI, adds HCl to acetylene: C₂H₂ + HCl → C₂H₃Cl. Modern plants start from ethylene and chlorine instead, then crack the intermediate: C₂H₄Cl₂ → C₂H₃Cl + HCl.
   > Two industries meet: PVC is where petrochemicals (the carbon) and chlor-alkali (the chlorine) come together.
27. **Note: Silicon from Sand**: checkmark *(after: Silicon)*
   > What: silicon metal is made by stripping oxygen from quartz (SiO₂) with carbon.
   > Chemistry: SiO₂ + 2C → Si + 2CO at around 2000 °C in an electric arc furnace.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Metallurgical grade: this gives silicon about 98 to 99% pure. Good enough for aluminum alloys and silicones, nowhere near good enough for chips.
   > The purity ladder: for electronics, silicon is turned into a liquid (trichlorosilane: Si + 3HCl → SiHCl₃ + H₂), distilled until almost perfectly clean, then turned back into silicon (the Siemens process). That reaches 'nine nines', 99.9999999%.
   > In the pack: quartz dust + coke dust in the EBF gives silicon for transistors and diodes. The next purity step comes at EV.
28. **Note: Growing a Perfect Crystal**: checkmark *(after: Semiconductor Silicon)*
   > What: chips are built on wafers sliced from one single crystal of silicon.
   > Chemistry: a seed crystal dipped into molten silicon and pulled up slowly while turning grows into an ingot where every atom lines up.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Why argon: molten silicon reacts with oxygen and nitrogen, so the crystal is grown under argon, an unreactive noble gas. That's why the pack asks for argon here.
   > Doping: pure silicon conducts poorly. A few atoms of phosphorus per million (one extra electron each) make n-type silicon; boron (one electron short) makes p-type. Where the two meet you get a diode, and stacks of junctions make transistors.
   > In the pack: EBF: silicon dust + a tiny pinch of iridium + argon → monocrystalline silicon, then the Cutting Machine slices it into wafers.
29. **Note: Fission Power**: checkmark *(after: Fission)*
   > What: a fission reactor splits uranium nuclei and uses the heat to make steam.
   > Chemistry: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + about 200 MeV. Mass numbers balance (236 = 141 + 92 + 3) and so do protons (92 = 56 + 36).
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Chain reaction: each split releases 2 to 3 neutrons. If on average exactly one causes another split, the reactor runs steadily. Control rods absorb extra neutrons to hold it there.
   > Where the energy comes from: the fragments weigh slightly less than the original nucleus. That missing mass becomes energy (E = mc²), about a million times more per atom than burning carbon.
   > Waste: the fragments are radioactive. In Mekanism, nuclear waste is processed into plutonium and polonium, which feed the next tiers. Always plan coolant and a SCRAM circuit.
30. **Note: Fusion Power**: checkmark *(after: Fusion)*
   > What: fusion joins hydrogen isotopes into helium. It powers every star.
   > Chemistry: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV. Per kilogram of fuel that's about four times more energy than fission.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > The hard part: nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. They must hit at enormous speed, which means a plasma at about 100 million °C, held away from the walls by magnetic fields or squeezed by lasers.
   > Ignition: laser fusion fires lasers into a tiny gold cylinder (a hohlraum) that turns the light into X-rays and crushes a fuel pellet. Mekanism borrows exactly that: a laser burst into a filled Hohlraum lights the reactor.
   > Fuel: deuterium comes from heavy water; tritium is bred from lithium: ⁶Li + n → ³H + ⁴He.
31. **Note: Antimatter as a Battery**: checkmark *(after: Antimatter)*
   > What: every particle has an antiparticle with the opposite charge. Meet and they annihilate into pure energy.
   > Chemistry: all the mass turns to energy: E = mc². One gram of antimatter meeting one gram of matter releases about 1.8 × 10¹⁴ J.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > Real antimatter: positrons (anti-electrons) are used every day in PET scans. Antiprotons and antihydrogen are made at CERN, but all of it ever made adds up to only nanograms, at an enormous energy cost.
   > A store, not a source: making antimatter always costs more energy than it gives back. That's why it works as a battery: put energy in once, carry it in a tiny pellet, get it out later.
   > In the pack: the SPS turns polonium and huge amounts of power into antimatter, which charges Antimatter Cores for the capstone. That part is game design, not real physics.
32. **Note: The Whole Notebook**: checkmark *(after: Seed of a New World)*
   > The last page of the notebook is blank. You realise you're meant to write it.
   > What: the Seed of a New World puts one product of every chemistry lesson into a single 9x9 recipe.
   > Chemistry: each ingredient stands for a whole industry you rebuilt from the ground up.
   > {@pagebreak}
   > The ledger: coke (pyrolysis and steelmaking), water and hydrogen (synthesis and electrolysis), sulfuric acid (the contact process), polyethylene (cracking and polymerisation), processing units (silicon purification and PVC), stainless plates (alloys), oganesson (building nuclei), plutonium and polonium (fission), Antimatter Cores (mass into energy).
   > The point: almost nothing in modern life is mined and used as-is. It's separated, reacted, purified and combined. That's chemistry, and now it's yours.
   > How: check JEI for the exact layout on the Ultimate Table.

   > Chemistry: osmium is the densest element (22.6 g/cm³). Gold is yellow and mercury is liquid because of relativity: their inner electrons move fast enough to change the orbitals' energies.
   > How: the PGM line gives platinum, iridium and osmium; the rest by dissolving or fusion (check JEI).
   > Tip: tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, 3422 °C.
32. **The d-Block: Period 7**: `chemlib:rutherfordium`; `chemlib:dubnium`; `chemlib:seaborgium`; `chemlib:bohrium`; `chemlib:hassium`; `chemlib:meitnerium`; `chemlib:darmstadtium`; `chemlib:roentgenium`; `chemlib:copernicium` *(after: The Actinides, Superheavy Elements)*
   > What: the superheavy transition metals, 104 to 112.
   > Chemistry: each was made a few atoms at a time by smashing nuclei together. Several are named after scientists: Rutherford, Seaborg, Bohr, Meitner, Röntgen, Copernicus.
   > How: only the Fusion Chamber makes these. Check JEI for pairs that add up.
   > Tip: seaborgium was named while Glenn Seaborg was alive, a rare honour.
33. **The Lanthanides**: `chemlib:lanthanum`; `chemlib:cerium`; `chemlib:praseodymium`; `chemlib:neodymium`; `chemlib:promethium`; `chemlib:samarium`; `chemlib:europium`; `chemlib:gadolinium`; `chemlib:terbium`; `chemlib:dysprosium`; `chemlib:holmium`; `chemlib:erbium`; `chemlib:thulium`; `chemlib:ytterbium`; `chemlib:lutetium` *(after: The d-Block: Period 6, Rare Earths)*
   > What: the whole lanthanide row, 57 to 71.
   > Chemistry: they fill the 4f orbitals, which sit deep inside the atom, so their chemistry is almost identical. That's why separating them takes hundreds of extraction steps.
   > How: press U on each element in JEI for Dissolver sources; fuse the rest in the Fusion Chamber. Promethium has no stable isotope.
   > Tip: four of them are named after one Swedish village, Ytterby: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium, erbium.
34. **The Actinides**: `chemlib:actinium`; `chemlib:thorium`; `chemlib:protactinium`; `chemlib:uranium`; `chemlib:neptunium`; `chemlib:plutonium`; `chemlib:americium`; `chemlib:curium`; `chemlib:berkelium`; `chemlib:californium`; `chemlib:einsteinium`; `chemlib:fermium`; `chemlib:mendelevium`; `chemlib:nobelium`; `chemlib:lawrencium` *(after: The Lanthanides, Actinides)*
   > What: the whole actinide row, 89 to 103. Every one is radioactive.
   > Chemistry: only thorium and uranium last long enough to be found in quantity. Everything past uranium was first made in reactors or in the debris of bomb tests.
   > How: dissolve uranium and thorium materials; fuse the heavier ones (check JEI).
   > Tip: americium is in most household smoke detectors.
35. **Every Box Filled**: checkmark *(after: The d-Block: Period 7)*
   > Every element, in a chest. You remember when this was how you made worlds.
   > What: you've collected every block of the periodic table.
   > How: click to claim. Keep the chest; a periodic table wall of item frames is a fine way to show it off.
   > Tip: the Combiner can now build almost any compound you can name.
36. **Tour: The Frozen North**: find biome `minecraft:snowy_plains`; find biome `minecraft:ice_spikes`; find biome `minecraft:snowy_taiga`; find biome `minecraft:grove`; find biome `minecraft:snowy_slopes`; find biome `minecraft:frozen_peaks`; find biome `minecraft:frozen_river` *(after: Iron Pickaxe)*
   > What: visit seven snowy biomes.
   > Chemistry: ice floats because water expands about 9% when it freezes: hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open hexagonal lattice.
   > How: walk in. A Nature's Compass finds each one.
   > Tip: powder snow on frozen peaks swallows players. Leather boots let you walk on it.
37. **Tour: Heat and Rain**: find biome `minecraft:desert`; find biome `minecraft:badlands`; find biome `minecraft:eroded_badlands`; find biome `minecraft:savanna`; find biome `minecraft:jungle`; find biome `minecraft:bamboo_jungle`; find biome `minecraft:mangrove_swamp` *(after: Tour: The Frozen North)*
   > What: visit seven warm biomes, from dry desert to jungle.
   > Chemistry: badlands terracotta gets its reds and oranges from iron oxides, the same rust you can make in the Combiner.
   > How: walk in. Badlands have gold at every height, so bring a pickaxe.
   > Tip: jungle temples and desert pyramids hold trim templates for the trim quests.
38. **Tour: Hidden Places**: find biome `minecraft:mushroom_fields`; find biome `minecraft:cherry_grove`; find biome `minecraft:lush_caves`; find biome `minecraft:dripstone_caves`; find biome `minecraft:deep_dark`; find biome `minecraft:old_growth_pine_taiga` *(after: Tour: Heat and Rain)*
   > What: the rare and underground biomes.
   > Chemistry: dripstone forms when water with dissolved calcium bicarbonate drips and loses CO₂, leaving calcium carbonate behind: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.
   > How: mushroom fields are islands far out at sea. Lush and dripstone caves sit under the surface; the deep dark sits below Y 0 under mountains.
   > Tip: no hostile mobs spawn on mushroom fields. Safe camping.
39. **Tour: Strange Lands**: find biome `biomesoplenty:redwood_forest`; find biome `biomesoplenty:lavender_field`; find biome `biomesoplenty:volcano`; find biome `biomesoplenty:mystic_grove`; find biome `regions_unexplored:bayou`; find biome `regions_unexplored:redwoods`; find biome `regions_unexplored:prismachasm` *(after: Tour: Hidden Places)*
   > What: seven biomes from Biomes O' Plenty and Regions Unexplored.
   > How: Nature's Compass lists modded biomes too. Prismachasm is a cave biome, so dig.
   > Tip: volcanoes have lava at the top. Bring fire resistance.
40. **Tour: The Five Fires**: find biome `minecraft:nether_wastes`; find biome `minecraft:crimson_forest`; find biome `minecraft:warped_forest`; find biome `minecraft:soul_sand_valley`; find biome `minecraft:basalt_deltas` *(after: Into the Fire)*
   > What: visit all five vanilla Nether biomes.
   > Chemistry: basalt is cooled lava, mostly silicates of iron and magnesium. Nether quartz is SiO₂.
   > How: walk in. Warped forests are the safest place in the Nether: endermen only.
   > Tip: ghasts hunt soul sand valleys. A shield blocks fireballs.
41. **Tour: The Deeper Fires**: find biome `biomesoplenty:crystalline_chasm`; find biome `biomesoplenty:undergrowth`; find biome `biomesoplenty:visceral_heap`; find biome `biomesoplenty:withered_abyss`; find biome `regions_unexplored:infernal_holt`; find biome `regions_unexplored:blackstone_basin` *(after: Tour: The Five Fires)*
   > What: Nether biomes from Biomes O' Plenty and Regions Unexplored.
   > How: Nature's Compass works in the Nether too. Withered abyss is a void: don't fall in.
   > Tip: crystalline chasm's crystals are pretty and brittle. Mine with care.
42. **Tour: The Void**: find biome `minecraft:the_end`; find biome `minecraft:end_highlands`; find biome `minecraft:end_midlands`; find biome `minecraft:small_end_islands`; find biome `minecraft:end_barrens` *(after: The Dragon's Breath)*
   > What: visit the five End biomes, from the central island to the outer islands.
   > How: after the dragon, throw an ender pearl into an end gateway to reach the outer islands.
   > Tip: end cities sit in the highlands. Bring slow falling against shulkers.
43. **Tour: Twilight Lowlands**: find biome `twilightforest:forest`; find biome `twilightforest:dense_forest`; find biome `twilightforest:firefly_forest`; find biome `twilightforest:clearing`; find biome `twilightforest:mushroom_forest`; find biome `twilightforest:enchanted_forest`; find biome `twilightforest:spooky_forest`; find biome `twilightforest:oak_savannah`; find biome `twilightforest:lake` *(after: The Twilight Forest)*
   > What: the Twilight Forest biomes you can walk into from day one.
   > How: walk in. The Magic Map shows biomes as you explore.
   > Tip: enchanted forests hold rainbow oak and the odd quest ram.
44. **Tour: Twilight Frontier**: find biome `twilightforest:swamp`; find biome `twilightforest:fire_swamp`; find biome `twilightforest:dark_forest`; find biome `twilightforest:dark_forest_center`; find biome `twilightforest:snowy_forest`; find biome `twilightforest:glacier`; find biome `twilightforest:highlands`; find biome `twilightforest:thornlands`; find biome `twilightforest:final_plateau` *(after: Tour: Twilight Lowlands, The Ur-Ghast, The Snow Queen)*
   > What: the Twilight biomes that open as you beat its bosses.
   > How: locked biomes hurt or block you until you beat the boss before them. Follow the Twilight boss order in Worlds.
   > Tip: the final plateau is the last place in the Twilight Forest. Enjoy the view.
45. **Tour: The Undergarden**: find biome `undergarden:forgotten_field`; find biome `undergarden:smogstem_forest`; find biome `undergarden:wigglewood_forest`; find biome `undergarden:gronglegrowth`; find biome `undergarden:frostfields`; find biome `undergarden:barren_abyss`; find biome `undergarden:ancient_sea`; find biome `undergarden:indigo_mushroom_bog` *(after: The Undergarden)*
   > What: explore the Undergarden's biomes.
   > How: walk in. Bring light: the Undergarden has no sun.
   > Tip: smog spires and smogstem forests are where you'll find the strangest mobs.
46. **Tour: The Otherside**: find biome `deeperdarker:deeplands`; find biome `deeperdarker:echoing_forest`; find biome `deeperdarker:overcast_columns`; find biome `deeperdarker:blooming_caverns` *(after: The Otherside)*
   > What: the four Otherside biomes from Deeper and Darker.
   > How: walk in. Sculk listens here too: sneak.
   > Tip: echo trees in the echoing forest give wood you can't get anywhere else.
47. **Tour: The Solar System**: find biome `ad_astra:lunar_wastelands`; find biome `ad_astra:martian_wastelands`; find biome `ad_astra:martian_canyon_creek`; find biome `ad_astra:martian_polar_caps`; find biome `ad_astra:venus_wastelands`; find biome `ad_astra:infernal_venus_barrens`; find biome `ad_astra:mercury_deltas`; find biome `ad_astra:glacio_snowy_barrens`; find biome `ad_astra:glacio_ice_peaks` *(after: Glacio, Mercury)*
   > What: stand in every planetary biome Ad Astra adds.
   > Chemistry: Mars is red from iron(III) oxide dust; Venus's clouds are sulfuric acid droplets, the same H₂SO₄ you make in the Contact Process.
   > How: fly to the Moon, Mars, Venus, Mercury and Glacio. Wear the right suit: Venus and Mercury need heat protection.
   > Tip: martian polar caps are frozen CO₂ and water in real life; in game, bring an oxygen supply.
48. **Element 5, Track 5**: `minecraft:music_disc_5`; 5x `chemlib:boron` *(after: The Creeper Collection)*
   > What: disc 5 and five boron. Boron is element 5.
   > Chemistry: boron is in borosilicate glass, which barely expands when heated. That's why lab glassware survives a flame.
   > Tip: the demigod finds this funnier than anyone else will.
49. **An Egg from the Past**: `minecraft:sniffer_egg` *(after: Dug-Up Trims)*
   > What: a sniffer egg, brushed out of warm ocean ruins.
   > How: place it on moss to hatch it faster. Adult sniffers dig up ancient seeds.
   > Tip: torchflowers and pitcher plants only come from sniffers.
50. **The Only One**: `minecraft:dragon_egg` *(after: Tour: The Void)*
   > What: the dragon egg. It teleports when you hit it.
   > How: push it off the portal with a piston, or let it fall onto a torch, then pick it up.
   > Tip: you'll need it for the Seed of a New World. Don't drop it in the void.

## The Demigod's Path (Main Questline)

### Getting Started

*You wake in a world you didn't make, with a god's patience and none of a god's power. A first day, a first night, first iron, and a first look at everything this world offers.*

1. **The Awakening**: checkmark *(after: Getting Started)*
   > You were more than this once. The book in your hands is in your own handwriting, though you don't remember writing it.
   > What: One idea stayed with you: everything is made of elements, and elements can be taken apart and put back together. This chapter gets you through your first day and night, to iron, and gives you a first look at the rest of the book.
   > How: Click the checkmark on the right to begin. Follow the lines: each quest leads to the next.
2. **Tip: Recipes and Jade**: checkmark *(after: The Awakening)*
   > What: JEI shows every recipe in the pack, including the ones changed for progression. Jade shows a small panel at the top of the screen for whatever block you're looking at.
   > How: Press R over any item to see how it's made, or U to see what it's used in. Try it on the crafting table you're about to make, then click the checkmark.
   > Tip: Type @modname in the JEI search bar to list a mod's items. When a machine isn't working, look at it: Jade shows its progress, energy and fluids, and usually why.
3. **Punch a Tree**: 16x any of `item_tag(minecraft:logs)` *(after: The Awakening)*
   > What: You start with nothing. Logs are the first thing you can take with bare hands, and everything early is made from them.
   > Chemistry: Wood is mostly cellulose, (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ, long chains of glucose, bound together by lignin, a tough aromatic polymer that keeps trees standing.
   > How: Hold left-click on a tree trunk. Any kind of log counts.
   > Tip: FTB Ultimine fells a whole tree at once: hold the ` key (grave/tilde) while you break the bottom log.
4. **Planks and a Workbench**: `minecraft:crafting_table` *(after: Punch a Tree)*
   > What: Planks are the basic building material for tables, tools, chests and beds. Your inventory only has a 2x2 grid; almost every tool and machine needs the full 3x3 grid of a crafting table.
   > How: Put a log in the 2x2 grid in your inventory: each log gives 4 planks. Then 4 planks in the 2x2 grid make the table. Place it and right-click it.
   > Tip: Keep a few logs as logs: some shortcuts below use them directly. The 8 torches in the reward get you through your first night.
5. **Somewhere to Put Things**: `minecraft:chest` *(after: Planks and a Workbench)*
   > What: You'll collect far more than you can carry. Chests hold 27 stacks each, and two side by side make a double chest.
   > How: 8 planks in a ring make one chest. The Utilitarian shortcut is better: 8 logs in a ring make 4 chests.
   > Tip: A chest is also the heart of your first backpack. That quest, and everything else about storage, is on the Storage and Logistics page.
6. **Messing About in Boats**: 1x any of `item_tag(minecraft:boats)` *(after: Planks and a Workbench)*
   > What: A boat crosses rivers and oceans much faster than swimming, and you can scout coastlines for villages and exposed ore.
   > Chemistry: Dry wood is about 0.4 to 0.7 g/cm³, lighter than water at 1.0 g/cm³, so it floats. That's density, nothing more.
   > How: 5 planks of one wood in a U shape. Check JEI for the chest boat too.
   > Tip: Mobs that touch a boat get pulled into it. Handy for moving a cow home.
7. **Sticks and a Wooden Pick**: `minecraft:wooden_pickaxe` *(after: Planks and a Workbench)*
   > What: Sticks are the handle of every tool and torch. A wooden pickaxe is weak, but it can mine stone, and stone is your next step.
   > How: 2 planks stacked vertically make 4 sticks. Then 3 planks across the top and 2 sticks down the middle of a crafting table make the pickaxe.
   > Tip: Utilitarian adds a shortcut: 2 logs stacked vertically make 16 sticks, twice as many per log as going through planks.
8. **Stone Age**: 16x `minecraft:cobblestone`; `minecraft:stone_pickaxe` *(after: Sticks and a Wooden Pick)*
   > What: Cobblestone makes stone tools, a furnace and a safe first shelter. A stone pickaxe can mine iron ore.
   > Chemistry: Stone is a mix of silicate minerals: quartz (SiO₂) and feldspars, aluminium silicates of sodium, potassium and calcium. Silicon and oxygen are the two most common elements in the Earth's crust.
   > How: Dig a few blocks down or mine a cliff face: stone drops cobblestone. The stone pickaxe is the wooden shape with 3 cobblestone in place of planks.
   > Tip: FTB Ultimine mines a whole vein at once. Hold the ` key (grave/tilde) while breaking blocks.
9. **Coal**: 8x `minecraft:coal` *(after: Stone Age)*
   > What: Coal fuels furnaces now, and becomes coke and steel in Chapter II.
   > Chemistry: Coal is plant matter buried for millions of years. Heat and pressure drove off most of its hydrogen and oxygen and left mostly carbon.
   > How: Coal ore is the black-speckled stone common in exposed cliffs and mountains. Mine it with any pickaxe.
   > Tip: Save extra coal for torches on your first mining trip. The Coke Oven in Chapter II eats a lot of it too.
10. **A Full Toolkit**: `minecraft:stone_sword`; `minecraft:stone_axe`; `minecraft:stone_shovel` *(after: Stone Age)*
   > What: A sword for the first night, an axe for faster wood, and a shovel for dirt, sand and gravel.
   > How: Each takes 1 to 3 cobblestone and 1 or 2 sticks. Press R on each one if you forget the shape.
   > Tip: An axe is also a decent weapon: it hits harder than a sword but swings slower.
11. **Bow and Arrow**: `minecraft:bow`; 16x `minecraft:arrow` *(after: A Full Toolkit)*
   > What: A bow lets you kill creepers and skeletons before they reach you.
   > How: 3 sticks and 3 string make a bow. Arrows are flint, a stick and a feather. Spiders drop string, chickens drop feathers, and gravel sometimes drops flint.
   > Tip: Hold right-click to draw the bow fully. A half-drawn shot does little damage.
12. **Fire**: `minecraft:furnace` *(after: A Full Toolkit)*
   > What: Fire is your first chemistry tool. It cooks food, turns sand into glass and ore into metal, and chars logs into charcoal (more on that in Chapter I).
   > Chemistry: A furnace drives reactions with heat. Most of what it does is breaking bonds and letting atoms find new partners.
   > How: 8 cobblestone in a ring make a furnace. Logs, planks, coal and charcoal all burn as fuel.
   > Tip: Furnaces in this pack cook about 4x faster than vanilla, so you rarely wait on one.
13. **Campfire**: `minecraft:campfire` *(after: Fire)*
   > What: A campfire cooks up to 4 pieces of food at once and never needs fuel.
   > Chemistry: A log on a campfire chars slowly without enough air to burn through: that's pyrolysis, the same reaction as the furnace, just slower.
   > How: 3 sticks, 1 coal or charcoal and 3 logs (check JEI). Right-click food onto it.
   > Tip: Utilitarian lets a campfire cook any log that burns into charcoal. Smoke rising from it also helps you find home.
14. **Glass**: 16x `minecraft:glass` *(after: Fire)*
   > What: Windows let you see out of your shelter, and glass shows up in many machine recipes later.
   > Chemistry: Sand is mostly silica, SiO₂. Melted and cooled quickly, it can't line up into crystals and freezes into a disordered solid: glass. Real glassmakers add soda (Na₂CO₃) to lower its melting point of about 1,700 °C.
   > How: Smelt sand in a furnace. Beaches, deserts and riverbeds are full of it.
15. **Light in the Dark**: 16x `minecraft:torch` *(after: Fire)*
   > What: Torches stop monsters spawning and light up caves.
   > Chemistry: A torch is combustion: carbon reacting with oxygen, C + O₂ → CO₂, releasing heat and light.
   > How: One coal or charcoal on top of one stick makes 4 torches. No coal yet? Smelt a log into charcoal: it works just as well.
16. **A Roof Overhead**: checkmark *(after: Light in the Dark)*
   > What: Monsters spawn in the dark. A small, lit, enclosed room keeps you safe while you work.
   > How: Build four walls and a roof from planks or cobblestone, add a door, and light the inside with torches. Click the checkmark when you're done.
   > Days here last about twice as long as in vanilla (roughly 20 minutes of daylight); nights are normal length, and rain is rarer and shorter.
   > Tip: Leave room to grow: your steam machines in Chapter I need floor space. The Building and Decoration page has ideas for later.
17. **A Bed**: 1x any of `item_tag(minecraft:beds)` *(after: A Roof Overhead)*
   > You never needed sleep before. Lying in the dark, you remember why mortals feared it.
   > What: Sleeping skips the night and sets your spawn point, so you wake up here if you die.
   > Chemistry: Wool is keratin, a protein held together by sulfur-sulfur bonds between cysteine units. The same protein makes up your hair and nails.
   > How: 3 wool of one colour over 3 planks. Shear sheep or kill them for wool.
   > Tip: Going exploring? A sleeping bag skips the night without moving your spawn (see the Quality of Life page).
18. **A First Field**: 1x any of `or(item(minecraft:wooden_hoe)item(minecraft:stone_hoe)item(minecraft:iron_hoe)item(minecraft:golden_hoe)item(minecraft:diamond_hoe))`; 8x `minecraft:wheat` *(after: A Bed)*
   > What: A small wheat field feeds you for the whole early game.
   > Chemistry: A plant builds itself out of air and water using sunlight: photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
   > How: Break grass and tall grass for seeds. Craft a hoe, till dirt next to water and plant them. Farmland stays wet up to 4 blocks from water. Harvest when the wheat turns golden.
   > Tip: Bone meal (from skeleton bones) is calcium phosphate, a real fertiliser. Right-click a crop with it to grow it faster.
19. **Sugar Cane**: 16x `minecraft:sugar_cane` *(after: A First Field)*
   > What: Sugar cane gives sugar for food and paper for books, maps and Silent Gear blueprints.
   > Chemistry: Table sugar is sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁: one glucose and one fructose joined together. Paper is pressed cellulose fibres, the same polymer as wood.
   > How: Find cane growing on sand or dirt right next to water. Plant it the same way to farm it; break the top and leave the bottom block.
   > Tip: Utilitarian makes paper in the 2x2 grid: 3 cane in an L shape give 3 paper.
20. **Something to Eat**: 2x `minecraft:bread` *(after: A First Field)*
   > What: Gods don't need to eat. You do, for now.
   > Chemistry: Baking turns starch and protein into new compounds. The brown crust comes from the Maillard reaction between sugars and amino acids.
   > How: 3 wheat in a row on a crafting table make 1 bread. With Utilitarian you can also put 3 wheat in an L shape in your 2x2 grid.
   > Tip: AppleSkin shows how much hunger and saturation each food restores.
21. **Cooked Meat**: 4x any of `or(item(minecraft:cooked_beef)item(minecraft:cooked_porkchop)item(minecraft:cooked_mutton)item(minecraft:cooked_chicken)item(minecraft:cooked_rabbit))` *(after: Something to Eat)*
   > What: Cooked meat restores far more hunger and saturation than bread. Cows also drop the leather you need next.
   > Chemistry: Heat denatures proteins: it unfolds them so they firm up, and turns tough collagen into soft gelatin. It also kills bacteria.
   > How: Kill cows, pigs, sheep, chickens or rabbits and cook the raw meat in a furnace, smoker or on a campfire. Any mix of cooked meat counts.
   > Tip: Breed animals with wheat (cows, sheep) or carrots (pigs) next to your base so you never have to hunt far.
22. **Gone Fishing**: `minecraft:fishing_rod`; 2x any of `or(item(minecraft:cooked_cod)item(minecraft:cooked_salmon))` *(after: Cooked Meat)*
   > What: A fishing rod gets you food anywhere there's water, plus the odd treasure.
   > How: 3 sticks and 2 string. Cast it into water and pull it in when the bobber dips. Cook the cod or salmon you catch.
   > Tip: A rod also reels in mobs and items, and fishing in the rain is faster.
23. **Leather Armour**: `minecraft:leather_chestplate`; `minecraft:leather_boots` *(after: Cooked Meat)*
